planting.note: Set out nursery starts or direct sow in fall to take advantage of winter rains, into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun near the coast or light shade inland.

directions: Red bush monkeyflower is a compact, evergreen subshrub native to coastal sage scrub and bluffs of San Diego County and northern Baja California, producing narrow, tubular flowers in shades of brick red to deep orange-red from spring through summer. Site it in full sun near the coast or light afternoon shade further inland, in lean, fast-draining soil, and withhold summer water once plants are established to avoid root rot. Hummingbirds visit the tubular blooms readily, and light shearing after the main bloom flush keeps the naturally sprawling growth habit tidy. It is more cold-sensitive than its relative sticky monkeyflower, so avoid hard frost pockets in zone 8b and below.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants into consistently moist to boggy soil in early spring; this creeping streamside native cannot tolerate drying out.

directions: Musk monkeyflower is a low, sprawling perennial native to streambanks, seeps, and wet meadows across western North America, spreading by rooting stems into loose mats studded with small, pale yellow, often maroon-flecked flowers through summer. Plant it in consistently moist to boggy, humus-rich soil in partial shade, such as at a pond margin or rain garden low point, since it cannot tolerate drying out. Historic garden strains were prized for a strong musky fragrance in the sticky, hairy foliage, though this scent has largely disappeared from modern seed-grown stock. Very cold hardy, it dies back in winter and resprouts readily from its creeping stems and roots each spring.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring, or in fall where winters are mild, onto lean, well-drained soil and rake lightly for good seed-to-soil contact.

directions: Threadleaf phacelia is a slender annual wildflower of dry sagebrush flats and open ground from British Columbia south to California and the Great Basin, bearing five-petaled, lavender-blue flowers in loosely coiled clusters above narrow, linear leaves. Direct sow in early spring or in fall where winters are mild, scattering seed onto lean, well-drained soil in full sun and raking lightly to ensure good seed-to-soil contact. Plants establish and bloom quickly in cool weather, tolerate poor and rocky soils, and need little supplemental water once seedlings are up. It is an excellent addition to pollinator and wildflower seed mixes, attracting native bees and small butterflies during its spring bloom period.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto bare, well-drained soil in full sun; summer-sown seed germinates poorly in warm soil.

directions: Sticky phacelia is a southern California native annual found in chaparral and open woodland of the Transverse Ranges, prized for electric gentian-blue, bell-shaped flowers with a contrasting white throat borne on glandular, sticky-hairy stems. Direct sow in fall onto bare, well-drained soil in full sun to take advantage of winter and early spring rains, since summer-sown seed germinates poorly in warm soil. Established plants need no supplemental irrigation and bloom heavily from April into June before setting seed and dying back with summer heat. The vivid flower color makes it a standout in native wildflower meadows, and it is heavily visited by native bees.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into gritty, sharply drained soil so winter cold and moisture break dormancy, or cold-moist stratify seed 4-6 weeks before an early spring sowing.

directions: Silky phacelia is a short-lived alpine and subalpine perennial of rocky slopes and open forest in the western mountains, forming a rosette of silvery, silky-haired leaves beneath dense, cylindrical spikes of deep purple flowers with conspicuous gold-tipped stamens. Sow seed in fall directly into gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun so that winter cold and moisture can break natural dormancy, or cold-moist stratify seed for four to six weeks before an early spring sowing. It thrives in rock gardens and high-elevation plantings that mimic its native talus and meadow habitat, and resents heavy, poorly drained, or overly fertile soil. Once established it needs only light supplemental water and tolerates severe winter cold without protection.
